article_title: Future technology workshop: A collaborative method for the design of new learning technologies and activities
citation: Giasemi N. Vavoula and Mike Sharples. (2007). Future Technology Workshop: A Collaborative Method for the Design of New Learning Technologies and Activities. Pre-print, to appear in International Journal of Computer Supported Collaborative Learning, Volume 2, Issue 4, December 2007. https://www.ftw.org.uk
title: Seven-session FTW sequence circling from far future through present to near future
description: The FTW is delivered as a series of seven sessions — Imagineering, Modelling, Role-play, Retrofit, Everyday, Futurefit and Requirements — each with a defined outcome recorded by facilitators. The sequence "starts in Box 4 in Table #2, examining new activity and technology in the far future", then circles through Boxes 3, 1 and 2 and back to 4, travelling from the far future to the present and near future. It is typically run as a half-day event with six to twenty participants plus two or three facilitators.
requirements: A minimum of six and maximum 20 participants plus two or three facilitators
Approximately two hours for the first four sessions and approximately 90 minutes for the remaining three
target_learners: children and adults participating in technology design workshops
target_learning_goals: envisioning future activities and deriving requirements for emerging technology
examples: Workshops on capturing and sharing visual events and on informal science learning used this session sequence with priming questions such as THINK SPACE AGE
key_sources: Giasemi N. Vavoula and Mike Sharples. (2007). Future Technology Workshop: A Collaborative Method for the Design of New Learning Technologies and Activities. Pre-print, to appear in International Journal of Computer Supported Collaborative Learning, Volume 2, Issue 4, December 2007. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9026-0

title: FTW toolkit for running Future Technology Workshops
description: An FTW toolkit is available for download at www.ftw.org.uk. It details "the structure of the workshop, the materials necessary for each session, and instructions for carrying out each session". The toolkit supports practitioners in replicating the seven-session method without prior specialist training in software design.
requirements: Low-tech prototyping materials such as Play-Doh, coloured pencils and paper, Post-it notes and sticky paper
target_learners: facilitators running participatory design workshops with children or adults
target_learning_goals: designing new learning technologies and activities through structured envisioning
examples: The toolkit documents session durations, researcher roles and observation-sheet formats used in the pilots

article_title: Effectiveness of flip teaching on engineering students' performance in the physics lab
citation: Gómez-Tejedor, J. A., Vidaurre, A., Tort-Ausina, I., Molina-Mateo, J., Serrano, M.-A., Meseguer-Dueñas, J. M., Martínez Sala, R. M., Quiles, S., & Riera, J. (2020). Effectiveness of flip teaching on engineering students’ performance in the physics lab. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103708
title: First-principles-based flip teaching design for laboratory sessions: pre-class videos for activation, in-class demonstration and integration phases.
description: The article describes an FT laboratory design in which students study documents and screencast videos before the session on the institution's online platform, so the session begins directly with experimental work. The learning design was based on the “first principles of instruction” following Lo, Lie, and Hew (2018): videos serve the activation phase, in-class measuring with teacher supervision serves the demonstration phase, and in-class organising, discussing and defending results serves the integration phase. Teacher explanations were reduced to answering doubts about out-of-class learning.
requirements: Students must study the pre-class documents and videos in advance; the article notes students realized after the first session that they needed to read and watch the materials beforehand.
constraints: The article could not trace how resources had been used in the FT courses, as no tracking tool was available on the platform at that time.
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students in technical degree courses
target_learning_goals: understanding of theoretical contents and experimental procedures
examples: Videos were screencasts explaining the lab work and equipment, e.g. a video introducing the free fall practice; groups of six uploaded a spreadsheet after each two-hour session and a report within ten days.
key_sources: Gómez-Tejedor, J. A., Vidaurre, A., Tort-Ausina, I., Molina-Mateo, J., Serrano, M.-A., Meseguer-Dueñas, J. M., Martínez Sala, R. M., Quiles, S., & Riera, J. (2020). Effectiveness of flip teaching on engineering students’ performance in the physics lab. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103708

article_title: Investigation of the Effects of Brain Teasers on Attention Spans of Pre-School Children
citation: Altun, M., Hazar, M., & Hazar, Z. (2016). Investigation of the Effects of Brain Teasers on Attention Spans of Pre-School Children. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(15), 8112-8119. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: FTF-K Attention Test for Children of Age 5-6 (Frankfurter Tests für Fünfjährige-Konzentration)
description: The FTF-K is a concentration test developed by Raatz and Möhling (1971) in which "children are asked to find and mark the pears among a mixture of apples and pears in 90 seconds". It was used as the measurement tool for attention spans in this study, administered individually or in small groups, with the pears marked within the time limit constituting the raw score. Reliability was established via test-retest with a correlation of r = 0.79.
requirements: Administered individually or in small groups by a researcher, in a silent room, with a stopwatch timing the 90-second marking period
constraints: Designed to measure concentration abilities of children of age 5-6
examples: Used as pre-test and post-test in small groups (5-10 children) in the presence of the students' teacher in a silent room
key_sources: Altun, M., Hazar, M., & Hazar, Z. (2016). Investigation of the Effects of Brain Teasers on Attention Spans of Pre-School Children. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(15), 8112-8119. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
